opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was kind of a simple realization at the time. I was around fourteen, and I was thinking about what I actually wanted to spend my life on. I didn't have some grand plan, but I kept coming back to this idea that if you could build systems that think, that can actually reason and solve problems, then that's sort of the last problem you'd ever need to work on directly. Every other thing I cared about, whether that's medicine, science, climate, whatever, would get dramatically easier if you had intelligence as a tool you could scale.

So it felt almost like leverage in its purest form. Instead of picking one field and spending forty years making a dent in it, why not work on the thing that could accelerate all of them? That logic just clicked for me, and once it clicked I couldn't really unsee it.

The other part is that I was just obsessed. I started reading everything I could find, papers I barely understood at first, online courses, implementing things myself and breaking them. There was this feeling that the field was early enough that a motivated kid with an internet connection could actually get to the frontier if they worked hard enough. That was incredibly exciting. It didn't feel like a career decision so much as finding the thing I couldn't stop thinking about, and then deciding to take it seriously.

r001.rationale: The candidate says scalable AI could make other fields easier and accelerate them, which made choosing AI over one field appealing. It does not clearly say he envisioned AI doing the work in those fields for him.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, at 14 it didn't feel like a choice so much as the only thing that made sense. I'd gotten obsessed with the idea that intelligence itself could be built, that you could sit down and write something that learns. Once that clicked for me, everything else seemed small by comparison. If you could build systems that could do science, that could solve problems faster than any person, then working on that was obviously the highest-leverage thing a person could do with their life.

I was also just very bored in school. I was teaching myself from papers and online courses, and I remember emailing researchers and being surprised when some of them actually wrote back. That gave me the sense that this field was open, that you didn't need permission to contribute, you just needed to do the work. So it felt right partly because of the scale of the ambition and partly because it was the first thing where I could see a clear path from curiosity to actually mattering. I never really looked back.

r001.rationale: The response says he was drawn to building intelligence that could do science and solve problems, but it does not explain that AI resolved indecision among valuable fields or that he could build a system to do those fields’ work for him.

astra-6.text: At 14, I was fascinated by the idea that we could build something that learns and solves problems. Intelligence is behind so much of what humans accomplish, so figuring out how to recreate even part of it felt like an incredibly important challenge. I didn’t have a detailed career plan. I just wanted to understand how it worked and start building things.

sol-6.1.text: At 14, I was drawn to the idea that intelligence itself was something we could understand and build. AI seemed like a way to work on that question while potentially helping solve a lot of other problems. I didn’t know exactly where it would lead, but that combination made it feel worth pursuing.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could help solve many problems, but it does not mention indecision among valuable fields or envisioning a system that would do work in those fields for him.
